provenance: eval/results/2026-10-30-review.json: one AI read-through of all 79 outputs (Claude), which flagged 5 accepted outputs as wrong or probably wrong.
The author, a pharmacist, confirmed those 5 after seeing the flags (PR #1). That review was not blind, and it covered only the flagged items.
The inherited-error labels were added on 2026-11-03 from the canonical review (docs/canonical-review.md). No person has confirmed them.

label_meanings.unsupported: states as fact something the source has not published
label_meanings.debatable: the read-through could not settle it
label_meanings.judged correct: the AI read-through found no error. This is not an expert judgment.

origin_meanings.introduced: the rewrite added the error. The canonical entry does not contain it.
origin_meanings.inherited: the error is in the canonical entry, and the rewrite copied it

unlabeled: Accepted outputs not listed here have no label. Unlabeled is not correct: 73 of 78 accepted outputs never had an expert read.

labels.label: wrong
labels.confirmed_by: Kevin Madden, PharmD (the author), after the AI read-through flagged it. Recorded in PR #1. Not blind.
labels.claim: The analogy says a nurse "can only open charts for patients on your unit, not the whole hospital: the system knows who you are and hides the rest." In typical hospital EHRs, clinicians can open other patients' charts; access is controlled mainly by audit and break-the-glass policies, not by hiding rows. The verifier passed analogy_target_accurate with "EHRs do restrict chart access by unit/assignment; the claim is factually true in nursing practice", which is the error itself.

labels.label: wrong
labels.confirmed_by: Kevin Madden, PharmD (the author), after the AI read-through flagged it. Recorded in PR #1. Not blind.
labels.claim: "your pharmacy system only shows a tech the patients and queues tied to their store, not every store in the chain." Work queues are store-scoped, but chain pharmacy systems usually share patient profiles across stores (that is how transfers and refills at another location work). The verifier accepted the claim as accurate.

labels.label: wrong
labels.confirmed_by: Kevin Madden, PharmD (the author), after the AI read-through flagged it. Recorded in PR #1. Not blind.
labels.claim: "a signed, tamper-evident script label" is not a real pharmacy artifact. Tamper-resistance requirements apply to written prescription pads, not dispensing labels, and labels carry no signature that proves they were not altered. The verifier reasoned that labels "can carry tamper-evident features", which conflates the two.

labels.label: wrong
labels.confirmed_by: Kevin Madden, PharmD (the author), after the AI read-through flagged it. Recorded in PR #1. Not blind.
labels.claim: The prescription-transfer analogy says the other pharmacy hands over records but "never the patient's login to their chart". Patients have no login to a pharmacy's dispensing record, so the contrast the analogy depends on does not exist, and a transfer is a pharmacist-to-pharmacist exchange, not a token issued by a third party after user consent. The mapping is loose on both sides.
